summary: Emil Kowalski explains how to decide when to animate and when not to. Every animation needs a purpose: explaining how a feature works, making a button press feel alive and responsive, avoiding a sudden appearance, keeping spatial consistency, or, for rarely used parts, delight. How often people will see an animation is a key factor: things used many times a day, hover effects and every keyboard-initiated action are best with no animation (keyboard actions should never animate). Unless it is a marketing site, animations have to be fast (UI animations generally under 300ms) because speed improves perceived performance and keeps the interface connected to the user's actions. For a design system this becomes a gate before any motion token is used (purpose, frequency, speed) plus concrete component behaviour for toasts, tooltips, dropdowns, command menus and spinners [inferred].
key_ideas: Animations done right make an interface feel predictable, faster and more enjoyable; done wrong they feel unpredictable, slow and annoying and can cost user trust.
Before animating anything, name its purpose.
An animation can replace a static marketing asset when it explains how a feature works right in the first viewport.
A subtle scale-down when pressing a button is a purposeful animation: it makes the interface feel alive and responsive.
Toasts should animate in, and entering and leaving in the same direction makes swipe-to-dismiss feel intuitive.
Delight animations work only on things people rarely use; used daily, the delight fades into irritation.
Frequency of use is a key factor in deciding whether to animate: something opened hundreds of times a day, like Raycast, is best with no animation.
Keyboard-initiated actions should never be animated because animation makes them feel delayed and disconnected.
Outside marketing sites, animations must be fast; they improve perceived performance and make the interface feel like it is listening.
A faster spinner makes loading feel faster even when the load time is the same.
Keep UI animations under 300ms as a rule of thumb; a 180ms dropdown feels more responsive than a 400ms one.
Tooltips need a slight first delay, but once one is open, neighbouring tooltips should open instantly with no animation.
Even a rarely used, purposeful animation still has to be checked for speed.
The goal is a great interface, not animation for its own sake; sometimes the best animation is no animation.

rules.rule: Before adding any animation, state its purpose (explain how something works, make an interaction feel alive and responsive, avoid a sudden appearance, keep spatial consistency, or delight); if it has none, do not animate.
rules.why: Done wrong, animations make an interface feel unpredictable, slow and annoying and can cost user trust; making sure an animation has a purpose is step one of knowing when to animate.
rules.evidence: Purposeful animations: "Step one is making sure your animations have a purpose"; "what’s the purpose of this animation?"

rules.rule: Do not animate for animation's sake; when an animation does not make the interface better to use daily, ship no animation.
rules.why: The goal is to build interfaces users will happily use daily; sometimes the best animation is no animation.
rules.evidence: Building great interfaces: "The goal is not to animate for animation’s sake"

rules.rule: Decide whether to animate by estimating how often the user will see the animation; the more often it is seen, the stronger the case for no animation.
rules.why: Frequency of use is a key factor: repeated animations turn from pleasant into annoying and slow users down.
rules.evidence: "How often users will see an animation is a key factor in deciding whether to animate or not"; "Think about what the user wants to achieve and how often they will see an animation"

rules.rule: Do not animate the opening of UI that people open hundreds of times a day, such as Raycast or a command menu; show it instantly.
rules.why: If it animated every time it opened it would be very annoying; Raycast has no animation at all and the author calls that the optimal experience. The source illustrates this rather than stating it as a rule; when the open is triggered from the keyboard, the must rule on keyboard-initiated actions applies.
rules.evidence: Frequency of use: "I use Raycast hundreds of times a day"; "That’s the optimal experience"

rules.rule: For goal-driven tools, design for the user's goal with no unnecessary friction instead of trying to delight them.
rules.why: When the user opens such a tool they have a clear goal and do not expect or need to be delighted.
rules.evidence: "I don’t expect to be “delighted”, I don’t need to be"

rules.rule: Do not animate hover effects on elements users interact with multiple times a day.
rules.why: A hover effect is nice, but used multiple times a day it would likely benefit the most from having no animation at all.
rules.evidence: "A hover effect is nice, but if used multiple times a day"

rules.rule: Never animate keyboard-initiated actions.
rules.why: They may be repeated hundreds of times a day, and animation makes them feel slow, delayed and disconnected from the user's actions.
rules.evidence: "The same goes for keyboard-initiated actions ... You should never animate them."

rules.rule: Do not animate the highlight when navigating a list with arrow keys (for example in a command menu); move it instantly.
rules.why: Arrow-key navigation is a keyboard-initiated action, which should never be animated; an animated highlight feels delayed compared to the keys the user presses.
rules.evidence: "use arrow keys to navigate through the list. Notice how the highlight feels delayed"

rules.rule: Give buttons a subtle scale-down effect while they are pressed.
rules.why: It helps the interface feel more alive and responsive.
rules.evidence: Purposeful animations: "subtle scale down effect when pressing a button"

rules.rule: Animate toasts in rather than making them appear suddenly.
rules.why: A toast suddenly appearing would feel off.
rules.evidence: Sonner’s enter animation: "Having a toast suddenly appear would feel off, so we animate it in"

rules.rule: Make a toast come from and leave in the same direction, matching its swipe-to-dismiss gesture (Sonner: swipe down to dismiss).
rules.why: Coming from and leaving in the same direction creates spatial consistency, which makes the swipe-down-to-dismiss gesture feel more intuitive.
rules.evidence: Sonner’s enter animation: "comes from and leaves in the same direction"

rules.rule: Use delight animations (such as a morphing component) only on components users rarely interact with.
rules.why: Rarely seen, the animation is a pleasant surprise and makes the experience unique and memorable.
rules.evidence: "This works as long as the user will rarely interact with it"

rules.rule: Do not put delight animations on components used multiple times a day.
rules.why: Used multiple times a day the component would quickly become irritating; the initial delight fades and the animation slows users down. Stated as a consequence rather than a rule.
rules.evidence: "Used multiple times a day, this component would quickly become irritating"

rules.rule: On marketing pages, consider an animation instead of a static asset when it explains how a feature works in the initial viewport.
rules.why: The animated version helps the user understand what the feature does straight in the initial viewport.
rules.evidence: Purposeful animations: Linear Product Intelligence, linear.app/ai

rules.rule: Keep every product UI animation fast; only marketing sites are exempt.
rules.why: Fast animations improve perceived performance, stay connected to the user's actions and make the interface feel as if it is truly listening.
rules.evidence: Perception of speed: "Unless you are working on marketing sites, your animations have to be fast"

rules.rule: Keep UI animation durations under 300ms.
rules.why: Stated rule of thumb; fast animations improve perceived performance and stay connected to the user's actions.
rules.evidence: "As a rule of thumb, UI animations should generally stay under 300ms"

rules.rule: Keep dropdown animations fast: a 180ms dropdown feels more responsive than a 400ms one.
rules.why: A 180ms dropdown animation feels more responsive than a 400ms one.
rules.evidence: "A 180ms dropdown animation feels more responsive than a 400ms one"

rules.rule: Even when an animation is rarely seen and has a clear purpose, still check its speed; passing the purpose and frequency checks does not exempt it.
rules.why: The article orders the decision as purpose, then frequency, then speed, and says a rare, purposeful animation still has to be thought about for speed.
rules.evidence: "even if your animation won’t be used too often and it fulfills a clear purpose, you still have to think about its speed"

rules.rule: Use a faster-spinning spinner for loading indicators.
rules.why: A faster spinner makes the app seem to load faster even though the load time is the same, improving perceived performance.
rules.evidence: Perception of speed: "a faster-spinning spinner makes the app seem to load faster"

rules.rule: Give tooltips a slight delay before they first appear.
rules.why: It prevents accidental activation.
rules.evidence: "tooltips should have a slight delay before appearing"

rules.rule: While a tooltip is open, open other tooltips on hover with no delay and no animation.
rules.why: It feels faster without defeating the purpose of the initial delay.
rules.evidence: "hovering over other tooltips should open them with no delay and no animation"

rules.rule: Judge a frequently used animation by toggling it against a no-animation version and asking which feels better if used hundreds of times a day. [inferred]
rules.why: The article's own demos pose this comparison to show how animation feels when repeated.
rules.evidence: Command menu demo: "Which one feels better if used hundreds of times a day?"

decisions.question: Should this interaction animate at all?

options.name: Animate
options.effect: Can explain a feature, make an interaction feel alive and responsive, avoid a sudden appearance, keep spatial consistency or bring delight.
options.when: The animation has a clear purpose and users see it rarely, or it prevents something from appearing abruptly (e.g. a toast).

options.name: No animation
options.effect: The UI responds instantly and feels connected to the user's actions with no friction.
options.when: Users see it multiple or hundreds of times a day (launcher, command menu, frequent hover), or it is keyboard-initiated.

decisions.recommendation: Animate only with a purpose; use no animation for every keyboard-initiated action, and lean to no animation for anything seen many times a day; sometimes the best animation is no animation.

decisions.question: How long should a product UI animation such as a dropdown take?

options.name: 180ms
options.effect: Feels responsive and connected to the click.

options.name: 400ms
options.when: Not recommended for product UI; the article only exempts marketing sites from the need to be fast [inferred].

decisions.recommendation: Keep UI animations generally under 300ms; the 180ms dropdown feels more responsive than the 400ms one.

decisions.question: Should a component get a delight animation, such as morphing?

options.name: Delight animation
options.effect: Makes the experience unique and memorable; a pleasant surprise.
options.when: The user will rarely interact with the component.

options.name: Plain, unanimated
options.effect: No irritation or slowdown with repeated use.
options.when: The component is used multiple times a day.

decisions.recommendation: Use delight only on rarely used components; used daily, the delight fades and the animation slows users down.

decisions.question: How should tooltips open when the user moves between several of them?

options.name: Slight delay on the first tooltip, then instant
options.effect: Prevents accidental activation, then feels fast while browsing neighbouring tooltips.

options.name: Same delay and animation every time
options.effect: Each subsequent tooltip waits and animates again, which feels slower [inferred].

decisions.recommendation: A slight delay before the first tooltip, then open other tooltips with no delay and no animation while one is open.

decisions.question: How should a toast arrive and leave?

options.name: Animate in, enter and leave in the same direction
options.effect: Creates spatial consistency and makes swipe-down-to-dismiss feel intuitive.

decisions.recommendation: Animate the toast in and have it come from and leave in the same direction.

decisions.question: On a marketing page, should a feature be shown with a static asset or an animation?

options.name: Static asset
options.when: When motion would not help explain the feature [inferred].

options.name: Explanatory animation
options.effect: Helps the user understand what the feature does straight in the initial viewport.
options.when: The feature's workings are easier to understand when shown in motion (Linear's Product Intelligence).

decisions.recommendation: Use the animation when its purpose is to explain how the feature works, as Linear did for Product Intelligence.

process.detail: Ask what the animation is for: explaining a feature, feedback on a press, avoiding an abrupt appearance, spatial consistency for a gesture, or delight. No purpose means no animation.
Work out how often users will see it. Rare: animation (even delight) is fine. Multiple or hundreds of times a day, or any keyboard-initiated action: no animation.
Think about what the user wants to achieve; goal-driven tools should have no unnecessary friction rather than delight.
Unless it is a marketing site, make the animation fast, generally under 300ms (a 180ms dropdown beats a 400ms one).
Toggle the animated and unanimated versions and ask which feels better if used hundreds of times a day, as the article's demos do [inferred].
Keep a slight delay before the first tooltip, but while one is open, open the others with no delay and no animation.

caveats: Self-promotion: a banner for the author's aiforui.dev course opens the page and the article ends with a plug for animations.dev; neither is a rule.

The page's interactive demos (morphing feedback, command menu toggle with J/K and Shift, spinners, dropdowns) do not survive text extraction; only their labels and surrounding text are available, so their exact motion values are unknown.
This article gives no numeric values for the button press scale, the tooltip delay or the spinner speed; other Emil Kowalski articles may.

300ms is stated as a rule of thumb ("generally"), and marketing sites are explicitly exempt from the need for fast animation. The 180ms versus 400ms dropdown is a comparison, not a prescribed exact value.
The Raycast example is the author's personal usage, offered as an illustration rather than measured data.

Publication date unknown. Some demo captions appear twice in the extracted text ("Imagine you interact with this list often during the day.", the Paste button label); this may be two demo variants or an extraction artifact.
The only media item is an Obsidian app icon from the demo list, which carries no design lesson and was not downloaded.
